title: a computed member name is evaluated by the scope that builds the object or class, so the coercion it performs charges that scope and not the member it names
notes: specification/requirements.mdx, 'Context Access': `Capability.context()` 'MUST add that class's nominal identity to the ENCLOSING FUNCTION's inferred R row', and 'Inference': 'Requirement inference MUST be transitive through ordinary calls.' The question this case settles is which function is the enclosing one. A computed member name is not part of the member: `{ [k]() {} }` evaluates `k` when the object literal is built, and the method it names may never be called at all. So the coercion of `k` — which runs its `toString` — belongs to the scope that builds the object, and that is the function the row must reach. WHY THIS CASE EXISTS: the nine spellings above the controls were fail-open on a backend that attributed the computed name to the member's own row, where nobody ever collected it, and the shape is deceptive precisely because the name is written INSIDE the braces of a function-valued member. The three controls are what identify the cause: `computedNameOnAnArrowValue`, `computedNameOnALiteralValue` and `computedNameOnAClassField` put the same coerced name in the same position with a value that is not a method, so there is no member function boundary to lose the row at — and both backends already charged those three. Nine wrong answers next to three right ones with the same name in the same syntactic slot is the evidence that the boundary, and not the computed name, was the cause. The nine are chosen to cover every member kind that introduces a function boundary in both container forms: object-literal method, getter, setter, async method and generator method; class method, getter, static method and async method. A fix that handles object literals and forgets classes, or handles methods and forgets accessors, turns this case red rather than passing on a subset. WHAT THIS CASE DELIBERATELY DOES NOT PIN: a computed name built from a `Symbol.toPrimitive` const binding, which is a measured residual on both backends — TypeScript itself erases that member into an index signature, so neither implementation can see it, and pinning it would state a rule the specification does not. It also does not pin the diagnostics' ORDER; the judge compares a sorted multiset. `messageContains` is declared once, on the first diagnostic, and holds the whole set to Db: twelve refusals at twelve positions are satisfied by code and position alone whatever capability the row actually named. The bare name is the smallest fragment that works on both backends, which render a row as `Db` and `{Db}` respectively. VERIFIED LOAD-BEARING, not assumed: mutating the LAST declared line from 99 to 100 — one line past the end of the array, which is what an off-by-one over the element list would produce — turns the case red on BOTH backends with the position diff printed, and the file was restored byte-identically (sha256 c4f55d171d45b43c2027bf10ab6addef11f96ced0eb9cc6be92f7095ad96640e before and after, that digest being this file's content at the moment the mutation ran — the sentence recording it is appended afterwards, so the shipped file necessarily hashes differently). The paired negative control is `coercion-members-that-never-run-charge-nothing`, whose seventh position is a computed member name that coerces nothing and must keep compiling AND RUNNING, so a fix that charges every computed name turns that case red instead of passing quietly.
